Ralph Venning
RALF VEN-ing
proper noun
English given name Ralph, from the Old Norse Ráðulfr, “counsel-wolf”; the surname Venning a West-Country place-name.

📖 Biblical Definition

Ralph Venning (c.1621–1674) was a Puritan minister of Devon stock, educated at Cambridge, who labored in London and was among the nearly two thousand faithful ministers ejected in 1662 for refusing to bow to the Act of Uniformity. He is chiefly remembered for his searching treatise on sin, first titled Sin, the Plague of Plagues and later The Sinfulness of Sin, a work that anatomizes transgression as the believer’s deadliest enemy. Venning’s aim was not to crush the conscience without remedy but to magnify the grace of Christ by setting forth the exceeding sinfulness of sin—that the soul, seeing sin’s true vileness against an infinitely holy God, might flee the more swiftly to the Redeemer. He held the Reformed conviction that sin is no mere weakness or misfortune but rebellion against the Most High, deserving wrath, and curable only by the blood of the Lamb. His pastoral tenderness joined to doctrinal severity marks the true physician of souls, who shows the wound before he applies the balm. Ejected and silenced by the world, Venning nonetheless ministered grace through his pen, teaching the church to hate what God hates and to prize the cross that alone removes guilt. His witness stands as a rebuke to every age that would make light of sin and so make light of the Saviour.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An ejected Puritan minister of London, author of The Sinfulness of Sin (formerly Sin, the Plague of Plagues), a classic anatomy of transgression.

expand to see more

RALPH VENNING, English Puritan minister (c.1621–1674), educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and a preacher in London.

Among the ministers ejected in 1662 for refusing conformity to the Act of Uniformity.

Author of Sin, the Plague of Plagues, afterward republished as The Sinfulness of Sin.

His treatise sets forth sin as the soul’s deadliest enemy and rebellion against a holy God (Rom 7:13).

He magnified the grace of Christ by exposing the true vileness of transgression.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 7:13 — "Was then that which is good made death unto me? God forbid. But sin, that it might appear sin, working death in me by that which is good; that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful."

Psa 51:4 — "Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest."

Rom 6:23 — "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."

1Jo 3:4 — "Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Venning’s doctrine of sin is recovered against an age that renames transgression as weakness, sickness, or social conditioning.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Venning’s great theme stands directly athwart the spirit of the present age, which will not call sin sin. Where Scripture and Venning name rebellion against a holy God, the modern temper substitutes “poor choices,” “mistakes,” or the fault of circumstance, and so dissolves guilt into mere misfortune. But a sin that is only sickness needs no Saviour, only therapy; Venning’s anatomy of the sinfulness of sin is the necessary cure for that flattery.

The lesson to recover is that sin must be seen in its true vileness before grace appears in its true sweetness. Venning showed the wound that the balm of Christ might be prized. A church that minimizes sin will inevitably minimize the cross; one that, with Venning, trembles at sin’s exceeding sinfulness will run the harder to the blood that washes it away.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name Ralph means “counsel-wolf” from the Norse; Venning is a West-Country English surname.

expand to see more

Ralph — from Old Norse Ráðulfr, “counsel” joined to “wolf.”

Venning, an English surname rooted in Devon and the West Country.

Plague, from the Latin plaga, “a blow, a stroke,” hence a deadly affliction.

Sin, from the Old English synn, used to render the Hebrew chatta’ah and Greek hamartia, “a missing of the mark.”

Sinfulness intensifies the noun, marking sin’s essential and exceeding wickedness (Rom 7:13).

Usage

"Ralph Venning taught the church to see sin as the plague of plagues."

"After his ejection in 1662, Ralph Venning ministered chiefly through his pen."

"No writer exposes the true vileness of transgression more searchingly than Ralph Venning."
